query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Nanoparticle stability under high‐temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions is governed by the extent of lattice strain induced by atomic size mismatch. Nanoparticles synthesized with a reduced atomic size mismatch (and hence lower lattice distortions) will form a more uniform solid‐solution structure and experience slower atomic diffusion, thereby better preserving their single‐phase chemical and structural integrity compared to those with higher mismatch.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi‐element, near‐equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles fabricated by a standard physical or chemical synthesis method that produces a homogeneous, single‐phase material.
generation.intervention: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticles: one set using an alloy design where the selected elements have relatively similar atomic radii (minimizing atomic size mismatch) and a control set with the standard element combination that exhibits a moderate spread in atomic sizes.
generation.conditions: Exposure to service conditions that include catalytic temperatures (approximately 773–1173 K) and thermoelectric operation ranges (approximately 473–1923 K) in inert or mildly reactive atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions (strain fields) arising from atomic size differences among the constituent elements.
generation.mechanism: Reduced atomic size mismatch minimizes lattice strain, which in turn elevates the kinetic barriers for atomic diffusion. This kinetic hindrance delays thermally activated phase segregation and sintering, thereby preserving the nanoparticles’ single‐phase structural and chemical uniformity under high-temperature exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature service conditions, nanoparticles synthesized with minimized atomic size mismatch will show significantly less evidence of phase segregation, sintering, or coarsening (as observed via structural and compositional analyses) compared to their standard counterparts with larger size disparities.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles produced with the standard near‐equiatomic composition that exhibit a moderate range of atomic sizes and associated lattice strain.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to operate effectively provided that (a) the constituent elements remain within solubility limits and (b) the thermal activation is sufficient to promote diffusion without triggering other dominating stabilization effects such as those arising from surface encapsulation or oxidation. In systems where intermetallic interactions or extreme processing conditions prevail, the influence of atomic size mismatch on stability may be less pronounced.
generation.uncertainty: While the anticipated trend is that lower atomic size mismatch enhances stability, the precise quantitative impact on diffusion rates and phase segregation kinetics remains uncertain and may be influenced by additional factors such as surface effects, synthesis history, and service atmosphere.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of near‐equiatomic nanoparticles under identical synthesis parameters except for the alloy design. Group 1 is synthesized using elements selected for low atomic size mismatch, while Group 2 uses a conventional elemental combination with a moderately larger spread in atomic sizes. Subject both groups to prolonged thermal aging at temperatures representative of catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) service conditions in an inert or mildly reducing atmosphere. Structural and compositional analyses (using XRD, TEM, and EDS) are then performed before and after thermal treatment.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to detect changes in phase purity or emergence of secondary phases
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for monitoring particle morphology and evidence of sintering or coalescence
Energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for assessing elemental homogeneity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles synthesized with reduced atomic size mismatch (Group 1) do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in structural and chemical stability (i.e., similar or greater levels of phase segregation, sintering, or compositional inhomogeneity) compared to the control group (Group 2) after thermal aging, then the hypothesis that reduced atomic size mismatch (and associated lower lattice strain) is the primary factor governing high-temperature stability would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted much attention in various fields with regard to applications as structural materials, biomaterials, supercapacitors, and catalysts., HEAs comprise mixtures of five or more metallic elements at near equiatomic ratios and form simple single solid-solution phases having lattice structures including face-centered cubic (fcc) and body-centered cubic (bcc)., The high configurational entropy of these alloys stabilizes the solid-solution phase such that this phase appears rather than an intermetallic phase or phase segregation., The severe lattice distortion in these materials that results from differences in the atomic sizes of the constituent elements also causes low atomic diffusivity. The unique synergistic effects resulting from combining multiple elements provide high specific strength, ductility, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability, such that HEAs are unique and fascinating materials. In recent years, many researchers have reported that HEA nanoparticles (NPs) having sizes on the nanometer scale (that is, in the range of 1 to 100 nm) show promise with regard to catalytic applications. Since the successful fabrication of the first-ever entropy- stabilized oxides, or, more general, high-entropy oxides (HEOs), such solid solutions have drawn much attention due to their unique compositional and structural features, namely, the extreme chemical disorder incorporated into single-crystal structures (). One representative example is that the metal ions in (Mg0.2Co0.2Ni0.2Cu0.2Zn0.2)O are unanimously divalent and randomly occupy the cationic sites in a rocksalt structure. These cations are coordinated by lattice oxygen in an octahedral configuration, even though Cu(II) and Zn(II) are usually four coordinated to oxygen atoms as, for example, in their binary oxides (). This stabilization of Cu(II) and Zn(II) in an unfavorable configuration is ascribable to the increased configurational entropy and a high solid solution temperature (, , ). Inspired by rocksalt HEOs, researchers have undertaken extensive work to develop diverse types of HEOs. HEOs in different crystal structures have been synthesized accordingly in the past decade, such as fluorite (, ), perovskite (), spinel (), bixbyite (), and pyrochlore (, ). The fabrication of semiconductor chips, nowadays essential for computing, communication, or transportation systems, is probably one of the most paradigmatic examples. drafts.hypothesis: Nanoparticle structural and chemical stability at high temperature is governed by the lattice strain induced by atomic size mismatch; specifically, nanoparticles composed of elements with lower atomic size differences will exhibit enhanced stability compared to those with higher mismatch, because reduced strain minimizes the driving force for phase segregation during thermal exposure.
drafts.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles synthesized with a controlled suite of elements, varying only in their degree of atomic size compatibility.
drafts.intervention: Synthesize two series of nanoparticles: one set using elements chosen for low atomic size mismatch, and a second set where one element is substituted by another with a significantly larger atomic radius to intentionally increase mismatch while keeping near-equiatomic composition.
drafts.conditions: Expose both series to catalytic operation temperatures (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric-relevant temperatures (473–1923 K) under inert or mildly reactive atmospheres to simulate service conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: Lattice strain arising from mismatched atomic radii at the atomic scale within the solid solution.
drafts.mechanism: Lower atomic size mismatch minimizes internal lattice strain, maintaining a uniform single-phase structure by reducing the thermodynamic drive for diffusion and elemental segregation. In contrast, nanoparticles with higher mismatch experience increased strain, which promotes phase segregation and the formation of secondary phases under prolonged thermal exposure.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature service, the low-mismatch nanoparticles will retain a homogeneous single-phase structure and stable chemical composition, whereas the high-mismatch nanoparticles will show signs of phase segregation (e.g., splitting of characteristic XRD peaks), altered morphology (e.g., increased grain boundaries or secondary phases), and surface compositional changes.
drafts.baseline: The baseline is the standard near-equiatomic nanoparticle system synthesized without intentional mismatch enhancement, expected to manifest moderate stability.
drafts.boundary: This effect is expected primarily under high-temperature service regimes; at lower temperatures or in conditions where diffusion is limited, the role of lattice strain may be less pronounced. Additionally, if the mismatch exceeds solubility limits during synthesis, other factors (such as the formation of distinct intermetallics) may dominate.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles: one series with elements chosen for low atomic size mismatch and another with one element substituted to increase the mismatch. Subject both series to prolonged thermal aging at 773–1173 K in a controlled atmosphere mimicking catalytic conditions. After aging, perform structural characterization (e.g., XRD, TEM) and compositional analysis (e.g., EDS, XPS).
measurements: XRD for phase purity and detection of peak splitting indicative of phase segregation
TEM for morphological examination of grain boundaries and secondary phase formation
EDS/XPS for surface and bulk compositional uniformity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both low-mismatch and high-mismatch nanoparticle series retain essentially identical single-phase compositions, morphologies, and chemical uniformity after thermal aging, then the hypothesis that lattice strain from atomic size mismatch governs high-temperature stability would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In multi‐element, near‐equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles, lower atomic size mismatch among constituent elements leads to a more uniform lattice with reduced local strain, which in turn raises the kinetic barrier to atomic diffusion and segregation. This stabilizes the solid‐solution structure under high‐temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions.
drafts.material_initial_state: Multi‐element, near‐equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles with a standard (unoptimized) spread of atomic sizes.
drafts.intervention: Synthesize sets of nanoparticles by specifically tuning the alloy composition to reduce the atomic size mismatch (e.g., selecting element combinations with more similar atomic radii) versus a control group with standard near‐equiatomic composition.
drafts.conditions: Exposing nanoparticles to catalytic operation temperatures (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric operation temperatures (473–1923 K).
drafts.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortion and strain fields arising from atomic size differences.
drafts.mechanism: Reduced atomic size mismatch leads to minimized local strain, which suppresses diffusion-mediated phase segregation and elemental segregation. This enhanced kinetic stabilization under high thermal load preserves the uniform solid-solution structure and thereby maintains functional properties.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles synthesized with a lower atomic size mismatch will show improved structural and chemical stability (e.g., minimal phase segregation as evidenced by consistent lattice parameters and homogeneous elemental distribution) and sustained catalytic/thermoelectric performance compared to baseline nanoparticles.
drafts.baseline: Nanoparticles produced with standard near-equiatomic compositions and a broader distribution of atomic sizes.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for metallic nanoparticles where configurational entropy is the dominant factor; in systems where other interactions (e.g., very strong intermetallic bonding or surface oxidation effects) prevail, the effect of atomic size mismatch might be overshadowed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of multi-element nanoparticles: one set with reduced atomic size mismatch (achieved by selecting alloying elements with relatively similar radii) and one control set with a standard compositional spread. Subject both sets to repeated high-temperature cycling within the catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) regimes.
measurements: Pre- and post-cycling X-ray diffraction (XRD) to determine phase purity and lattice changes
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with elemental mapping to assess structural integrity and homogeneity
Catalytic activity or thermoelectric performance tests to monitor functional properties
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles with the adjusted (reduced) atomic size mismatch do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in structural and chemical stability (i.e., similar or greater degrees of phase segregation or performance degradation compared to the control group), then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: The degree of local chemical short‐range ordering (SRO), developed during synthesis, governs whether near‐equiatomic HEA nanoparticles maintain their single‐phase structure and chemical homogeneity under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric service conditions by limiting atomic mobility and suppressing phase segregation and sintering.
drafts.material_initial_state: As‐synthesized multi‐element solid-solution nanoparticles in a near-equiatomic composition that exhibit a high level of overall configurational disorder but with variable degrees of local SRO.
drafts.intervention: Control the cooling rate (or post-synthesis annealing protocol) after nanoparticle formation to intentionally promote stronger local SRO in one sample group versus minimal SRO in a control group.
drafts.conditions: Service conditions representative of catalytic operations (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric applications (473–1923 K), where high temperature promotes atomic diffusion.
drafts.structural_mediator: Local chemical short-range order in the nanoparticle lattice.
drafts.mechanism: Enhanced SRO creates local atomic motifs that impede atomic diffusion, reducing the driving force for elemental segregation and sintering. This stabilization delays or prevents phase separation and maintains a uniform single-phase structure under thermal stress.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles synthesized (or annealed) to develop higher SRO will show lower rates of sintering, reduced phase separation, and preserved homogeneity after prolonged exposure to high-temperature conditions relative to nanoparticles processed with rapid quenching (minimal SRO).
drafts.baseline: Nanoparticles produced with fast cooling (limiting the formation of SRO) are expected to experience more pronounced atomic diffusion, leading to phase segregation, coarsening, and compromised catalytic/thermoelectric performance over time.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism is anticipated to operate in HEA systems with near-equiatomic compositions where elemental size mismatches and enthalpic interactions are moderate. It may not apply to systems with strong immiscibility or where other stabilization mechanisms (e.g., core–shell encapsulation) dominate.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of near-equiatomic HEA nanoparticles using an identical precursor mix but varying only the cooling protocol immediately after synthesis. Group A will undergo slow cooling or controlled low-temperature annealing to favor SRO formation, while Group B will be quenched rapidly to suppress SRO. Both groups will then be subjected to prolonged thermal treatment simulating service conditions (e.g., 800 K for 100 hours).
measurements: High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) to assess particle size and evidence of sintering or phase segregation.
X-ray diffraction (XRD) to determine phase purity and detect any secondary phases.
Energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for compositional homogeneity.
Catalytic or thermoelectric performance tests before and after thermal treatment.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles in Group A (high SRO) do not exhibit significantly less sintering, phase segregation, or performance degradation relative to Group B (low SRO), then the hypothesis that local chemical SRO is the primary mediator for thermal stability will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Nanoparticles that retain a maximally disordered, near‐equiatomic solid‐solution structure are stabilized against high‐temperature phase segregation because the lattice distortions arising from the large atomic size differences and chemical randomness create high activation barriers for atomic diffusion.
drafts.material_initial_state: Multi‐element, near‐equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles synthesized by physical or chemical methods with a homogeneous, single-phase structure and full configurational disorder.
drafts.intervention: Prepare a controlled set of nanoparticles in which slight deviations from the ideal equiatomic ratio (thereby inducing measurable short-range ordering, SRO) are intentionally introduced, while keeping all other synthesis parameters identical to the baseline preparation.
drafts.conditions: Exposure to service temperatures of 773–1173 K for catalytic operations and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric applications, in inert or reducing atmospheres that minimize additional oxidation effects.
drafts.structural_mediator: The high lattice distortion and local strain fluctuations induced by the random occupancy of differently sized atoms, which kinetically hinders atomic diffusion and suppresses phase segregation.
drafts.mechanism: In a fully disordered, high-entropy nanoparticle, the varied atomic sizes and chemical identities produce a rugged energy landscape that dramatically increases the activation energy for atomic motion. This retards atomic diffusion and prevents thermally driven phase segregation and/or sintering, thereby preserving both the structure and chemical homogeneity. In contrast, even a slight emergence of local short-range order reduces these lattice strain effects, lowering the kinetic barriers to diffusion.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under service regimes, the fully disordered nanoparticles (baseline) will maintain their single-phase structure and chemical uniformity longer than those with induced short-range order. In the intervention samples, early signs of phase segregation or sintering (e.g., formation of secondary phases, increased particle coalescence) are expected relative to the baseline.
drafts.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized with the ideal near‐equiatomic, fully random composition expected to exhibit high lattice distortion and minimal atomic diffusion during high-temperature operation.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism is most relevant for multi-element systems where the constituent atomic sizes differ sufficiently to induce strong lattice distortions. In systems with minimal size mismatch or under conditions where external oxidation/passivation dominates, other stabilization factors may override this effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticles under identical synthesis conditions: one set with near‐ideal equiatomic composition (maximal configurational disorder) and a second set with a controlled deviation from equiatomic composition to induce short-range order. Heat both sets under identical simulated service conditions (e.g., 900 K in a controlled inert/reducing environment) for an extended period while monitoring structural evolution.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to detect phase segregation or the emergence of secondary phases
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) combined with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to monitor particle morphology and elemental homogeneity
Catalytic activity measurements over time to assess performance retention
Surface analysis (e.g., XPS) to ensure that observed changes stem from internal diffusion rather than surface oxidation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles with induced short-range order display stability (no increased phase segregation, sintering, or performance degradation) equal to or superior to the baseline fully disordered nanoparticles, then the hypothesis that lattice distortion from high configurational entropy governs stability under high-temperature service conditions is falsified.
